impacts.caseName: A.L.M. Holding Company v. Zydex Industries Private Ltd.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a patent owner that licenses exclusive commercialization rights but retains the right to sue third parties for infringement has sufficient constitutional standing to bring an infringement suit.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's dismissal for lack of standing, holding that the patent owner retained an exclusionary right sufficient to satisfy Article III's irreducible constitutional minimum of standing despite having granted an exclusive license. The court found that the retained right to sue was not rendered illusory by the rights granted to the licensee.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent owners structuring license agreements can retain standing to enforce patents against third parties by preserving exclusionary rights such as the right to sue, even after granting broad exclusive commercialization licenses.

impacts.caseName: Teva Pharmaceuticals International GmbH v. Eli Lilly and Company
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court erred in granting judgment as a matter of law that Teva's headache patents claiming methods of using humanized anti-CGRP antagonist antibodies were invalid for failure to satisfy the written-description and enablement requirements of 35 U.S.C. § 112.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's JMOL of invalidity for Teva's headache patents covering methods of treating headache with humanized anti-CGRP antagonist antibodies, after a jury had found willful infringement by Eli Lilly and no invalidity. The reversal reinstates patent protection for a significant class of migraine treatments, directly impacting competition in the multi-billion-dollar CGRP antibody drug market.
impacts.positiveImplications: Strengthens patent holders' ability to defend genus claims in the biopharmaceutical space where the specification discloses known methods of making and using antibodies, supporting broader patent protection for biologics.
impacts.negativeImplications: Generic and biosimilar competitors like Eli Lilly face continued patent barriers for CGRP-based migraine treatments, potentially delaying market entry and maintaining higher drug prices.

impacts.caseName: International Medical Devices, Inc. v. Cornell
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether plaintiffs presented legally sufficient evidence to establish that each of four asserted trade secrets was a protectable trade secret under California law, and whether the same analysis affected related patent inventorship and breach-of-contract claims.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the denial of JMOL on trade secret misappropriation claims, holding there was insufficient evidence that the asserted trade secrets were protectable under California law because the information was generally known. The court also reversed on patent invalidity, finding that the purported inventive contribution was based on the same generally known ideas, and reversed the breach-of-contract claim tied to the same confidential information.
impacts.positiveImplications: Defendants in trade secret cases benefit from clearer standards requiring plaintiffs to demonstrate that claimed secrets are not generally known in the relevant field, limiting overreach in trade secret litigation.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies asserting trade secret misappropriation must ensure robust evidentiary support that their claimed secrets are truly novel and not generally known, or risk losing related patent and contract claims as well.

impacts.caseName: Ollnova Technologies Ltd. v. Ecobee Technologies ULC
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court erred in using a single verdict form question covering infringement for all asserted patents, and whether the § 101 eligibility analysis for patents directed to building automation system wireless communications was properly conducted.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated an $11.5 million infringement and damages judgment and remanded for a new trial, finding that the single-question verdict form on infringement across multiple patents was prejudicially flawed. The court also remanded for further § 101 proceedings on one patent while affirming eligibility of two others. This decision reinforces the requirement for patent-specific jury findings in multi-patent cases.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers benefit from the requirement that verdict forms distinguish among asserted patents, preventing catch-all infringement findings that obscure which patents were actually infringed.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders asserting multiple patents face increased procedural requirements for jury instructions and verdict forms, potentially complicating trial strategy and increasing litigation costs.

impacts.caseName: AGI SureTrack LLC v. Farmers Edge Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether claims directed to automated systems for capturing, processing, and sharing farming data using passive data collection devices on farming equipment are patent-eligible under 35 U.S.C. § 101, and whether the district court erred in declining to find the case exceptional under 35 U.S.C. § 285.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed that AGI's farming data collection and sharing patents were directed to patent-ineligible abstract ideas under § 101 but vacated and remanded the district court's determination that the case was not exceptional, potentially opening the door to attorneys' fees for the defendant. The decision is significant for agricultural technology companies relying on patents covering data collection and processing methods.
impacts.positiveImplications: Technology companies accused of infringing data-processing patents in the agtech space may more readily obtain § 101 invalidity rulings and may also recover fees in exceptional cases.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders in the agtech and IoT data-processing space face heightened § 101 eligibility risks, and the remand on exceptionality signals potential fee-shifting exposure for asserting weak patents.

impacts.caseName: Insulet Corp. v. EOFlow, Co. Ltd.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the statute of limitations under the Defend Trade Secrets Act had expired before Insulet brought suit alleging misappropriation of trade secrets related to its insulin patch pump technology.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's denial of JMOL and held that Insulet's DTSA claim was time-barred, finding that Insulet knew or should have known of the misappropriation more than three years before filing suit. The decision reversed a jury verdict and damages award related to trade secrets allegedly misappropriated by former employees who helped a competitor develop a rival medical device.
impacts.positiveImplications: Companies accused of trade secret misappropriation can use statute of limitations defenses where the plaintiff had early knowledge of the alleged misappropriation, limiting exposure from delayed enforcement actions.
impacts.negativeImplications: Trade secret owners must act promptly upon learning of potential misappropriation or risk losing their DTSA claims entirely, even where significant damages may exist.

impacts.caseName: VLSI Technology LLC v. Intel Corporation
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court erred in granting summary judgment of noninfringement of a multicore processor patent based on extraterritoriality and rejection of a doctrine of equivalents theory, and whether the court properly struck certain damages theories.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed in part Intel's summary judgment of noninfringement of VLSI's multicore processor patent, finding genuine disputes of material fact regarding extraterritoriality and doctrine of equivalents. The court affirmed other aspects of the ruling. This case is part of the high-profile VLSI-Intel patent litigation involving billions of dollars in potential liability across multiple proceedings.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders asserting claims against semiconductor companies benefit from the court's willingness to find factual disputes precluding summary judgment on extraterritoriality and equivalents theories.
impacts.negativeImplications: Technology companies like Intel face continued exposure to patent infringement claims even where key manufacturing or design steps occur abroad, as the extraterritoriality defense is fact-intensive.

impacts.caseName: Constellation Designs, LLC v. LG Electronics Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patents claiming non-uniform constellations for digital communication systems are patent-eligible under 35 U.S.C. § 101, and whether the damages award and infringement findings were supported.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the summary judgment of patent eligibility for certain asserted patent claims related to non-uniform signal constellations used in digital communications, while affirming eligibility for other claims. The court also affirmed infringement and damages findings. The decision has significant implications for the telecommunications standards-essential patent landscape.
impacts.positiveImplications: Standards implementers like LG gain another opportunity to challenge eligibility of foundational communication technology patents, potentially reducing royalty exposure.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders in the wireless communications space face renewed § 101 challenges even after jury verdicts, creating uncertainty around the enforceability of patents covering mathematical optimization methods embedded in industry standards.

impacts.caseName: Versata Software, LLC v. Ford Motor Company
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court erred in excluding Versata's trade secret damages expert and in its judgment on breach of contract damages related to Ford's development of competing manufacturing configuration software.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the trade secret damages judgment and remanded for a new trial, instructing the district court to reconsider two previously rejected damages models. The court also reversed the breach of contract damages ruling, reinstating the jury award. The case involves Ford's alleged misappropriation of Versata's automotive configuration software trade secrets used in vehicle manufacturing.
impacts.positiveImplications: Trade secret plaintiffs benefit from the court's willingness to require reconsideration of damages models, expanding the range of permissible theories for quantifying misappropriation harm.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies that develop internal replacements for licensed software face heightened trade secret and breach of contract risk, particularly where the development overlaps temporally with the license period.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a Rule 30(b)(6) corporate representative may testify beyond personal knowledge for purposes of summary judgment, and whether the on-sale bar under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. § 102(b) requires that a prior art sale expressly disclose the device's functionality.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed summary judgment of invalidity under the on-sale bar, holding that Rule 30(b)(6) corporate representative testimony is admissible at summary judgment even when the witness lacks personal knowledge, and that the on-sale bar does not require express disclosure of a device's functionality at the time of sale. The decision clarifies the evidentiary standard for proving prior art sales.
impacts.positiveImplications: Defendants challenging patent validity benefit from broadened use of 30(b)(6) testimony to establish prior art sales and from the holding that commercial sales of a device trigger the on-sale bar regardless of whether functionality was publicly disclosed.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders face increased invalidity risk from historical product sales by third parties, even where the seller's current employees lack personal knowledge of the product's development.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the ITC properly found a Section 337 violation based on Apple's importation and sale of Apple Watch models incorporating blood oxygen measurement technology covered by Masimo's patents.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the ITC's finding that Apple violated Section 337 by importing Apple Watches with blood oxygen sensing features that infringed Masimo's patents, upholding the limited exclusion order barring importation. The court found no error in the Commission's domestic industry determination, validity rulings, or infringement findings in this high-profile dispute between two major technology companies.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders with domestic manufacturing or R&D operations can effectively use ITC proceedings to obtain exclusion orders against major technology companies importing infringing products.
impacts.negativeImplications: Major technology companies face significant supply chain and product availability disruptions when ITC exclusion orders are affirmed, potentially forcing product redesigns or royalty negotiations.

impacts.caseName: Ascendis Pharma A/S v. BioMarin Pharmaceutical Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether an ITC respondent may obtain a mandatory stay under 28 U.S.C. § 1659(a)(2) of a refiled declaratory judgment action after missing the deadline for seeking a stay of the original action involving the same parties and issues.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit held that an ITC respondent cannot circumvent the statutory deadline for seeking a mandatory stay by dismissing and refiling its declaratory judgment action. The decision prevents gamesmanship in parallel ITC and district court proceedings and preserves the ability of ITC complainants to pursue timely district court relief, particularly important in pharmaceutical patent disputes.
impacts.positiveImplications: Pharmaceutical patent holders filing ITC complaints benefit from assurance that respondents cannot manipulate statutory stay deadlines through strategic dismissal and refiling of declaratory judgment actions.
impacts.negativeImplications: ITC respondents who miss the 30-day deadline for seeking a mandatory stay of parallel district court proceedings cannot cure the missed deadline by refiling, limiting their procedural options.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court properly approved a $125 million class action settlement of claims that the federal judiciary overcharged PACER users by using fees to fund unrelated court technology systems, and whether the attorneys' fees and incentive awards were appropriate.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the approval of a $125 million nationwide class action settlement resolving claims that the judiciary charged excessive PACER fees in violation of the E-Government Act. The court upheld attorneys' fees awards and incentive awards to class representative nonprofits, rejecting objections on jurisdiction, settlement fairness, and Supreme Court precedent on incentive awards.
impacts.positiveImplications: The settlement provides substantial reimbursement to hundreds of thousands of PACER users, including law firms and businesses, and confirms that class settlements involving government fee overcharges can proceed under the Little Tucker Act.

impacts.caseName: Fortress Iron, LP v. Digger Specialties, Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patents are invalid for omission of a coinventor when the patent holder acknowledges the coinventorship but cannot locate the omitted inventor to correct the error under 35 U.S.C. § 256.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed that patents were invalid due to omission of a coinventor where the patent holder acknowledged coinventorship but was unable to locate the missing inventor to effectuate correction. The court also affirmed the denial of correction under § 256(b), highlighting the critical importance of properly identifying and maintaining contact with all contributors to an invention.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers can defend on inventorship grounds even where the patent holder acknowledges the error, if correction procedures cannot be completed.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies collaborating with foreign manufacturers on product development face invalidation risk if they fail to identify and maintain contact with all potential coinventors, particularly overseas contributors.

impacts.caseName: Federal Express Corporation v. Qualcomm Incorporated
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the PTAB's obviousness determination was supported where the IPR petition was filed by a third party (Qualcomm) that was not a party to the underlying district court litigation on the same patent's filing deadline for the actual defendant.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the Board's obviousness determination and remanded for further proceedings, raising concerns about the circumstances under which a non-party to the underlying litigation filed IPR petitions on the actual defendant's statutory deadline. The decision has implications for the practice of third-party IPR filings and potential coordination between accused infringers and third-party petitioners.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders gain greater scrutiny of potentially coordinated third-party IPR filings that may circumvent the one-year time bar of 35 U.S.C. § 315(b).
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies that file or benefit from third-party IPR petitions face increased risk that such petitions will be scrutinized for improper coordination with the actual defendant in related litigation.
